title: Keep a steady pulse
summary: Repeat {{first}} with quarters, eighths and rests.
goal: Place separate attacks on written beats and half-beats while counting through rests.
body:
First practice open strings. Use open string 6 throughout. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”; the metronome marks the numbers. A quarter takes one beat and an eighth half a beat. A rest still takes time. Start at 60 BPM, count aloud, then play. Repeat at the same tempo before trying 70 BPM.

Tuning: {{tuning}}. Strings 6 → 1: {{openStrings}}. Reference A4 = {{reference}} Hz. Select your actual tuning in Settings → Instrument or in Tuner. Changing the profile updates this lesson; it does not physically tune the guitar.

In the steps, {{openExample}} (6/0) means sounding note {{openExample}}, string 6, fret 0. String 1 is the thinnest; 0 means open. Read the displayed positions for your selected tuning. Pitch labels use chromatic enharmonic names. Audio measures audible pitch and attacks, not your finger or string choice.

Use a clean input from your guitar interface, or choose the acoustic microphone/pickup source explicitly. Play one note at a time and stop the previous string. Choose Practice for a signal check and count-in. Without reliable calibration, rhythm and overall scores remain unavailable. Review measured pitch or missed-attack feedback before increasing the tempo.

quarter-pulse.title: 1. Count the quarter-note bar
quarter-pulse.body: Bar 1: play on 1, rest on 2, play on 3 and 4. {{positions}}.

quarter-space.title: 2. Count through the rest
quarter-space.body: Beat 2 lasts one complete click interval. Stop the sound and do not pluck.

eighth-pairs.title: 3. Divide the first two beats
eighth-pairs.body: Bar 2: play on “1” and “and”, rest on “2”, play on “and”. {{positions}}.

eighth-spaces.title: 4. Leave space between attacks
eighth-spaces.body: Finish bar 2: play on “3”, rest on “and”, play on “4”, rest on “and”. {{positions}}.

whole-pattern.title: 5. Play both bars
whole-pattern.body: Eight attacks, including repeated notes; every written note needs a fresh pluck. {{positions}}.
